On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased by 0.2% compared with July.

The Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), the measure used for comparisons across the Eurozone and which the ECB targets, also rose 2.9% annually and 0.2% monthly, matching the national CPI reading.

A key driver behind the increase was the rise in energy costs.

Energy prices climbed 10.5% from a year earlier, significantly faster than the 8.3% increase recorded in July and the 3.4% rise seen in June.

Meanwhile, underlying inflation remained more contained.

Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy components, is estimated at 2.4% y/y in August.

The market reaction has been rather muted to the data, as interest rate expectations remained unchanged.

How sticky is inflation? Let's see: The state readings released around the same time: Bavaria August CPI +2.9% vs +2.8% y/y prior Saxony August CPI +2.9% vs +2.7% y/y prior North Rhine Westphalia August CPI +2.9% vs +2.7% y/y prior Baden Wuerttemberg August CPI +2.6% vs +2.5% y/y prior And even the monthly estimates are showing stronger prints after the big jump in July: Bavaria August CPI +0.2% m/m Saxony August CPI +0.2% m/m North Rhine Westphalia August CPI +0.2% m/m Baden Wuerttemberg August CPI +0.1% m/m That in itself continues to reaffirm that price pressures are growing more broadly, not just driven by base effects for the most part.

Based on the estimates above, we should see the overall German national print later come in around 2.9% or 3.0% (rounded up) - so that sort of fits with estimates of 2.95% (3.0%).

Again, this doesn't change anything for the ECB going into September but it at least reinforces the narrative that a positioning move is needed by the central bank.

They are poised to raise key interest rates again so as to bring monetary policy to a mildly restrictive stance.

That in order to prepare themselves for a battle against inflation and potential second round effects that could materialise late this year or early next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Unemployment remained stuck at 4.9pc in the three months to June, while the number of payrolled employees fell by 13,000, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics.

Economists had predicted that the unemployment rate would ease to 4.8pc.

Unemployment jumped to 5.4pc in June, up from 4.6pc the previous month.

Meanwhile, vacancies dropped to 707,000 in the three months to July – the lowest level since 2021 – with a particular strain on entry-level job openings.
